intro.text: A number sign (#) is used with this entry because of evidence that spermatogenic failure-104 (SPGF104) is caused by homozygous mutation in the CCDC9 gene on chromosome 19q13.32.

checks.claim: Spermatogenic failure-104 (SPGF104) is caused by homozygous mutation in the CCDC9 gene.
checks.evidence_quote: we identified a novel homozygous variant in CCDC9 (NC_000019.9: g.47763960C>T, NM_015603.3, NP_056418.1: p. Ser109Leu) in a patient from a consanguineous family
checks.explanation: Paper reports a homozygous CCDC9 variant in severe asthenozoospermia but frames CCDC9 only as a candidate gene ('may be'); the SPGF104 designation is not in the paper.

checks.claim: The CCDC9 gene is located on chromosome 19q13.32.
checks.explanation: Chromosomal location is standard nomenclature. The paper's coordinate places the gene on chromosome 19.

paragraphs.text: Spermatogenic failure-104 (SPGF104) is a form of male infertility. Sha et al. (2019) described it as severe asthenozoospermia, in which very few spermatozoa are motile and the spermatozoa have badly damaged morphology and ultrastructure.

checks.claim: Spermatogenic failure-104 (SPGF104) is a form of male infertility.
checks.evidence_quote: severe asthenozoospermia is a serious threat to the male reproductive health
checks.explanation: The abstract refers to male reproductive health, not explicitly to infertility, and does not name SPGF104.

checks.claim: SPGF104 presents as severe asthenozoospermia, in which very few spermatozoa are motile.
checks.evidence_quote: Owing to less than 1% of motile spermatozoa in the ejaculated semen, severe asthenozoospermia is a serious threat to the male reproductive health.
checks.explanation: Defines severe asthenozoospermia by very low sperm motility.

checks.claim: In SPGF104, the spermatozoa have badly damaged morphology and ultrastructure.
checks.evidence_quote: its morphology and ultrastructure were severely damaged in the spermatozoa containing the novel variant
checks.explanation: The abstract describes severely damaged sperm morphology and ultrastructure.

paragraphs.text: Sha et al. (2019) reported a man from a consanguineous family who had severe asthenozoospermia. Fewer than 1% of the spermatozoa in his ejaculate were motile, and his spermatozoa showed severely damaged morphology and ultrastructure.

checks.explanation: The <1% figure is given as the general definition of severe asthenozoospermia, not as a measurement from this patient.

paragraphs.text: Sha et al. (2019) identified a novel homozygous variant in the CCDC9 gene (g.47763960C-T, NM_015603.3) in a man with severe asthenozoospermia from a consanguineous family. The variant resulted in a ser109-to-leu (S109L) substitution, and in silico analysis predicted it to be highly pathogenic. CCDC9 protein levels were significantly reduced in the patient's spermatozoa. The authors suggested that CCDC9 may be a novel pathogenic gene for severe asthenozoospermia.

paragraphs.text: Khan et al. (2025) performed whole genome sequencing on 26 individuals (3 to 5 per family) from 7 large families from rural Pakistan with clinically diagnosed male infertility. Five of the families had a history of consanguinity. The authors identified plausible genetic causes in 5 of the 7 families (71%). In one of these families, they identified biallelic missense substitutions in the CCDC9 gene. In the other families, they found variants in other genes: a homozygous 10-kb deletion of exon 2 of M1AP, biallelic missense substitutions in SPAG6 and in TUBA3C, and an in-frame hemizygous deletion in the X-linked TKTL1 gene.
